I think this is a problem that existed even before. If you look closely, AI just accelerates everything—both the pros and the cons. It seems to be an inherent problem with the academic system itself.

Signals are inherently bound to be distorted. The "legitimate methods" conceived by humans and social signals are easy to manipulate. Because public data like the number of published papers and diplomas act as strong social signals, they end up being distorted. This is known as Goodhart's Law.

The problem is that if this persists long-term, there will eventually be a shortage of personnel to quantitatively evaluate papers, and society probably won't hire these researchers. There is also no incentive to hire them, as verification rarely leads to direct profit. People tend to want to be the starting point of a discipline; they generally do not like checking other people's work.

As a result, academia will increasingly be validated solely by "which lab, which advising professor, and what peer network certified you." The value of the offline world will rise, simply because digital costs have become too cheap.

Soon, research quality and social status will likely merge again, resembling the Middle Ages. Even if we assume someone has actual research capabilities, if evaluators do not invest enough time in verification, the system will inevitably revolve around the more prestigious labs.

I suspect there will be a flood of research applying AI, but the topics of these studies will likely be quite narrow and localized (it would be nice to have statistics on this). I believe the overall diversity of topics explored across academia will diminish.

For this reason, I think existing networks will only grow stronger.

I feel that any solutions to this problem will go awry. I doubt self-purification is even possible anymore. Established researchers protect the monopoly power of publishers, while those existing publishers generally just want to cut costs. The authority of these publishers must be protected by the established researchers who have already secured their positions.

Next, the system that used to manipulate the number of papers will probably shift into a system that manipulates network reputation. The competition to get into good labs and the strategies to secure co-authorships with famous researchers will simply become the new means of competition.

As an aside, as someone who studied more on the pure math side, Blums speed up theorem is rather intuitive. It looks like there might be a relatively elegant proof using topology. Blums speed up theorem is basically just a statement that the set of programs that implement a particular computable function doesn’t satisfy the greatest lower bound property. This is also the case for, for example, the set of rational numbers: there exist subsets of the rational numbers with a lower bound but not a greatest lower bound (like the set of all positive rational numbers q where q^2 >= 2). 'static lifetime bounds are kind of confusing in Rust, but here goes: A 'static lifetime constraint on T says: types that satisfy T must not contain any borrowed value/content whose lifetime will be shorter than the life of the program. So suppose you have a string s, and Option<&String> q. If q has the constraint 'static, and you do q = Some(&s) this should be rejected by the compiler since a reference to s gets a shorter lifetime than 'static by default (you could do q = Some(&'static s) if s is say a string literal or a leaked box but not for a normal string). In the examples it looks like you have to use a tuple to trick the borrow checker but the concept is the same: Rust allowed violation of the 'static lifetime bounds. The drop implemenation demonstrates it: drop happens in reverse declaration order, so the string s gets dropped first. "Information density" is a ratio, i.e. the ratio between the amount of information and the length, area or volume in which it is stored, so it does not "scale".

The amount of information at high enough amounts scales with the volume in which it is stored.

Because of the need to be able to reach the cells that store information, the density of information is normally high in 2 directions an low in the 3rd direction.

This is why it is useful to distinguish between the density of information per area, which is determined by things like the size of a magnetic head or the resolution of a photolithographic process, and the density of information per volume, which is determined by the density of information per area and by some kind of layer thickness, which is usually determined by mechanical considerations, e.g. to ensure enough strength for a tape or a disk or an integrated circuit package.

Like I have said, at high enough amounts of information you reach an almost constant information density per volume, like in a rack full with HDDs or in a magnetic tape robotic library.

Ordinary memory is not a list. It's a flat space read in O(1).

In theory. In practice there are multiple levels of cache, and cached reads will be much, much faster than main memory reads.

So if your entire data structure lives in cache and you repeatedly loop through it, it's going to be processed much more quickly than a bigger and more spread-out structure.

There's also paging, and alloc/dealloc to consider, and maybe garbage collection.

Hi HN, I'm Joshua. rply is an open-source inbox between you and your AI agents.

Rply is not meant to be remote control for sessions. Instead you get a control center to communicate with your remote agents, have them send you notifications, ask questions, share progress and expose full UIs for you to monitor progress.

I built it for an SEO agent I run unattended on a VM. I initially glued it together with ntfy for push notifications, an exposed site for seeing status and a cron monitored inbox for waking the agent. This worked but I kept setting it up for new projects and it became unwieldy.

Rply now is much simpler. The agent gets a cli, you get a simple container to host on the same VM or just connect to the hosted version for free. Your agent sends cli commands and sets them up to wake it when you send messages. It can send questions, files to show you it's work and ask for secrets and receive them without ever seeing them. What I also love is that it can set up apps for a channel which get their data from your VM. You can view your stats, see recent work, monitor the agents, etc.

ntfy is an amazing project and inspired this heavily. But what was missing is the back and forth communication with the agent, formatted questions, artifacts and bringing all that in one place. Rply strives to be as simple as ntfy while being built for agents.

It is still an early project but it's working well for a lot of projects already. I would love to hear your feedback, open to any critique or improvements you have!

Right now there are only arrangements for my instrument, tuba, but I’d love to add more instruments like ocarina or bassoon in the future. I started this because over the 10 years I have played tuba, I probably went through all free tuba resources on the internet multiple times and many pieces I wanted to play I did not even find for tuba.

I’m working completely alone on this, so to be honest with you: I got a lot of AI help. Basically the pipeline for getting a public domain piece onto my website is downloading a well scanned score from a library like IMSLP, then a couple of Claude subagents read through it bar by bar and write the tuba part from it. A script checks for clashes with the piano accompaniment and a separate Claude session proofreads the result against the scan. Then I play it through myself, look through the sheet music and double check weird passages with other sources on the internet. Most of the time there are maybe 2 errors left in a big piece like the Can-Can, so the subagents already do a great job!

The sheet music player is rendered by alphaTab. It had some bugs that I patched, at some point I want to send them the fixes so they can fix them in alphaTab itself too. I also got a recording feature, there I had a big problem with the piano accompaniment coming through the speaker and tried to subtract it from the recording, but it still doesn’t work too well sadly. Lately I rewrote my page turn logic to do half page turns, cause every musician knows how frustrating it is to not see the next notes until the page turns.

I would agree with OP with "stay away".

The Google paper Towards Modern Development of Cloud Applications[0] does a great job explaining why.

TL;DR the case they make against micro-services architectures (which Lambda encourages):

    1. It hurts performance
    2. It hurts correctness
    3. It is hard to manage
    4. It freezes APIs
    5. It slows down application development
For even a moderately complex system, spreading logic out over multiple discrete runtimes doesn't make sense; instantly run into each of the 5 points. The only times I've found functions useful is truly single-point behavior where we were running some logic connected to CloudFront on each request for some header parsing.

It is certainly possible to write a monolith in Lambda as well, but then that would be bad architecture and a bad fit and I suppose why they are now introducing this new model that is more like GCP Cloud Run or Azure Container Apps.

[0] https://sigops.org/s/conferences/hotos/2023/papers/ghemawat....

title: Show HN: I found a new planetary candidate in Kepler Data with AI

Hey HN! I was playing around with the Kepler and TESS data last weekend when I hacked around a way to pixel-peep stars dimming periodically to potentially find new exoplanets with Codex.

I ended up running the engine to find an interesting signal in Kepler data that was uncatalogued with a dip repeating every 13.77 days around KIC 5689121, a red dwarf in Lyra about 970 light-years away. If it's a planet, it'd be roughly 2.5–3 times Earth's radius !

Funnily enough, this candidate is just 7.1 arcseconds from a much brighter neighbour (KIC 5689116) and is very hard to see because of how much brighter it is (probably why it went unnoticed for so long)

Of course, there's work to do before calling it confirmed - my TRICERATOPS analysis is about 6.9% and we have to get IR/AO / Keck observations to prove it's out there ! (which I'm honestly intimidated by but cautiously optimistic about because I've never worked in non-CS adjacent research) but I found the activity of making cool tools to potentially discover things about our universe quite fun !

I think at this scale that it's cleaner to think of the grid as a flywheel system of enormous (~infinite) mass. Every consumer (home, factory, business, whatever) and every producer (home solar, nuke plant, wind machine, whatever) is connected to this flywheel system, and they're all in parallel (just like circuits in a home are).

Take power out of the flywheel? Sure, why not -- that's exactly what we've done with it at home since we had an AC grid to speak of.

Try to impart higher voltage to put power back into the system? Fine, no worries. Flywheel just accepts and absorbs whatever you put into it as long as it has the right shape.

Try to change the flywheel's AC frequency or waveform, though? Hah, fat chance: Flywheel will trip your breakers or reduce your gear to ash -- whichever comes first. We play by the flywheel's rules, and those rules aren't optional at all. It may be just a big dumb flywheel, but the flywheel's enforcement is absolute.

Anyway, it's a big mythical flywheel. We get charged money to take power out of it, and (with the right arrangements) we get paid money to put power into it.

And by design, grid-tied inverters are quite good at following the flywheel's rules. They match the flywheel's waveform very well [lest they go poof]. They can only put power into that flywheel, and they reject power from that flywheel. The inverter is a one-way thing that, from a high-enough viewpoint, looks kind of like a check valve or a diode does.

---

But it's not an ideal, perfect system. It does not exist in a world of frictionless pulleys and ropes that don't stretch.

That imperfection shows up in the wires and transformers connecting the house to that flywheel system, in that these parts have a non-zero impedance. (For the sake of this discussion, impedance can mean about the same thing as resistance)

And that impedance is useful. It means that we can increase voltage a very tiny bit on our local leg, and thereby succeed at using our puny little solar power system to help cover our own local base load.

Suppose our plug-in solar widget can produce 800 Watts today. The plug-in kit increases the voltage that it drives that plug with until 800 Watts of power output is achieved (which is only a very tiny amount of extra voltage, but it's real anyway). This is its purpose: Where some robots pass butter, this robot puts 800 Watts into a power socket.

Since the wiring between the plug-in solar and the local household baseload stuff has a lower impedance than the path to the mythical flywheel does, our baseload stuff (the fridge, the router, the fan by the window) gets first dibs at that 800 Watts of minutely-enhanced voltage.

If we produce more than we use, the excess local power production gets provided to and soaked up by the flywheel (maybe we get paid for that).

If we use more than we produce, then the deficit is made up for by the flywheel (and we definitely pay for it).

If our generation and consumption is perfectly balanced (which never really happens), then the flywheel plays no real part in the program except to provide a waveform for our solar inverter to synchronize with.

---

Anyway, it's not new tech at all. It's safe in that it won't work at all without a connection to the big flywheel in the sky. And folks have been using grid-tied inverters for quite a long time, but that was done on a dedicated circuit (with a dedicated breaker or fuse or RCBO or whatever they're called wherever you are).

But there's still some new stuff going on: It can be a plug-in system that works without individual planning or permitting; in some places, a person can legally buy and use a kit without obtaining extra permission.

The safety of sharing a circuit is also important, since enhanced potential exists for overheating things. Germany limits their plug-in solar to 800 Watts, or about 3.5A @ 230V, while their circuits are usually 16A.

That means there could be as much as 19.5A of nominal current flow within a circuit before some combination of circuit breaker or inverter limit is reached.

I learned a long time ago to never question a German about their electrical standards, though, so I can only assume that very smart people have worked very long hours to see that this situation is safe-enough.

Some more technical details.

CLI

The CLI is written in Go. Interpreted/VM approaches (specifically Python/Java) felt more involved (particularly at install time) for what was intended to be a lightweight, easy to install utility. Being able to output executable binaries was really important, and the high level language looked nice (I'm new to Go).

There's no library (yet) - it's a CLI tool. My thinking is that a lot of the file management functionality has to talk to the file system (gigabyte files are technically doable, currently capped at 100MB while we work out the issues). The more I thought about adding multiple programming languages and flexible (stream to file, to string, to byte array) interfaces, the harder to use it looked; offloading concerns like memory usage and hash verification to the developer. With that said, there will be an API (I'm working on it now), and it'll have all the capabilities/interfaces of the CLI, but obviously be a roll-your-own logic situation. On the CLI, I really like how minimal the integration is - you write one file poller (examples in the docs) and you're basically done with the "get the data" problem and onto the more interesting "use the data" problem. It is a bit of an unusual approach though.

I'm considering adding a callback command to the CLI that triggers after each payload is written, that would make integration even simpler and help scripts trigger appropriately.

API

The clients (just the CLI at the moment) subscribe to a websocket to listen to files being published (one for each subscription). This is the one technical decision that took me the most time. Long poll / regular poll were both considered and discarded due to the fairly heavy impact it has on LB billing when scaled out, particularly for heavy clients with high frequency polls. Directly exposing a Kafka queue had its own issues, and would have pushed the architecture to be a shape I wasn't a fan of for a public service (less auth control, looser control of server balancing, client version tie-in, etc).

Downloads are via a signed link - this allows us to control access to the CDN and prevent us being flooded with requests from a given IP or account. I'm solo and self-funded so controlling spend is critical for us at the moment.

Validation

We do some basic checks for XML and JSON (e.g. XXE and other attacks) in all published files and we'll build up more checks and more data types over time. No file is visible to subscribers until it has passed validation.

What's planned

Priority 1 is on-boarding publishers so we have useful data on the site.

General polish is high on the list (anything UX or DX - CLI, API, site usability)

Show HN: Stream live open data in two commands
text:
A service and open source tool to get open data streams in two commands. No sign up needed for subscribing.

Streams to try:

- https://hypermass.io/stream/_J0fm450s - extreme UV images of the sun from SOHO - visual data

- https://hypermass.io/stream/_ATtCoEK - GDACS live disaster data (filtered to just the ongoing items)

The CLI (Apache 2.0, https://github.com/hypermass-io/hypermass-cli) tool allows you to subscribe to multiple live streams of files, with the files arriving in a local folder. The filenames are ULIDs so they can be easily sorted into time order in scripts and code. Publishing works similarly - drop files into a folder and they get read, published and deleted locally. The idea is that by being highly opinionated about the shape of the data (files, delivered in sequence, in real time) a bunch of the logic and edge cases get handled well in one place (things like ordering, retries, hash verification, reconnection, etc) - rather than requiring every subscriber to implement it themselves for every source.

A high-speed version for things like departure boards, train positions is in the pipeline.

Background: About 10 years ago, I worked for a few years supporting and developing some of the UK Rail Open Data systems. As a developer I was frustrated at how fragmented the open data space was, and how every open data system was designed as a blank-page exercise. I realised that a lot of data falls into an odd middle ground, too infrequent to economically poll on a large scale, too large for messaging protocols, but in some sense still real time. For example transport schedules, periodic solar imagery, disaster alerts - real-time but infrequent.

Fairly often I just wanted a "just give me the data" option when the solutions I found were static catalogues with no nod towards real-time use, bespoke APIs, analytics systems and other things I didn't need.
